easy.prompt: A video promises “free Robux if you enter your password here.” What should you do?

choices.text: Enter my password to get the free Robux
Ignore it — real currency is never free from outside links
Share it with a friend so they get free Robux too
Enter a fake password just to see what happens

easy.hint: Think about who actually benefits if you type in your real password.
easy.explanation: No legitimate site or video can give you free in-game currency — the real goal is almost always to steal your login.

easy.prompt: A “loot box” in a game costs real money for a random reward. What is this most similar to?

choices.text: A vending machine
A slot machine / gambling
A library book
A gift card

easy.hint: Think about what you're actually paying for — a guaranteed item, or a random chance at one?
easy.explanation: Loot boxes use randomized rewards for money, the same mechanic as gambling — several countries now regulate them as such.

easy.prompt: Someone offers you a “rank boost” if you just give them your password “really quick.” This is:

choices.text: A nice gesture from a helpful player
Always a scam — no real admin needs your password
Fine as long as they seem friendly
Only risky if they ask more than once

easy.hint: Would a real moderator or support account ever actually need your password?
easy.explanation: No legitimate moderator, admin, or support account will ever ask for your password — this is one of the oldest scam tricks in gaming.

easy.prompt: A message says “Hurry! This offer expires in 2 minutes!” This kind of pressure is:

choices.text: Proof the offer is real and limited
A common scam tactic to stop you from thinking it through
Only used by legitimate stores
Something to ignore only if you're over 13

easy.hint: Scammers want you to act before you think — why would urgency help them do that?
easy.explanation: Fake urgency (“hurry,” countdown timers, “limited time”) is a classic scam tactic designed to stop you from pausing to check if something's real.

hard.prompt: An account claiming to be “verified customer support” DMs you first about a billing issue. What's the red flag?

choices.text: Nothing — support often reaches out first
Real support never DMs you first — you have to contact them
It's fine if the account has a logo
It's only a scam if they ask for money upfront

hard.hint: Who usually starts the conversation when you actually need help from a real company?
hard.explanation: Legitimate support teams respond to tickets you open — they essentially never DM you first out of the blue.

hard.prompt: You see a QR code sticker on a vending machine promising a “free prize.” What's the safest move?

choices.text: Scan it — QR codes are always safe
Don't scan unknown QR codes in public places — verify the source first
Scan it only if it has a cartoon on it
Scan it, then close the page fast if it looks wrong

hard.hint: Could someone have placed a fake sticker over a real QR code?
hard.explanation: “QR code swapping” is a real scam — a fake sticker is placed over a legitimate code to redirect you to a malicious site.

hard.prompt: Someone asks you to resolve an “urgent account problem” by buying a gift card and sending the code. Why is this always a red flag?

choices.text: Gift cards are a normal way to pay any company
Legitimate organizations never ask to be paid in gift cards
It's fine if the amount is small
It's only suspicious if they ask for more than one card

hard.hint: Gift cards are nearly untraceable once the code is shared — who benefits from that?
hard.explanation: Gift cards are a scammer favorite because once the code is handed over, the money is essentially gone and untraceable — no real company asks to be paid this way.

hard.prompt: What's the single best habit to protect yourself from most online scams?

choices.text: Trusting any offer that looks professional
Pausing to verify through an official source before acting
Acting fast before an offer expires
Asking other players in the game if it's real

hard.hint: Think about what nearly every scam in this topic relied on to work.
hard.explanation: Almost every scam tactic — urgency, fake authority, too-good-to-be-true prizes — only works if you act before verifying. Pausing to check is the strongest defense.

easy.prompt: An AI chatbot gives you an answer in a very confident tone. Does that mean it's correct?

choices.text: Yes, confidence means accuracy
No — AI sounds equally confident whether right or wrong
Only if it's a paid AI tool
Only for math questions

easy.hint: Does AI have a built-in “I'm not sure” voice that sounds different from its confident voice?
easy.explanation: AI chatbots state wrong answers in the exact same confident tone as correct ones — always double-check anything that actually matters.

easy.prompt: You use AI to explain a homework concept you're stuck on, in your own words after. Is this cheating?

choices.text: Yes, any AI use is cheating
No — using AI to understand something is learning, not cheating
Only if a teacher finds out
Only for essays, not math

easy.hint: What's the difference between using a tool to understand something, versus copying its full answer?
easy.explanation: Using AI to explain a concept you're stuck on is learning. Copy-pasting its full answer as your own is cheating.

easy.prompt: A video appears to show a friend saying something they never actually said. What could this be?

choices.text: Definitely real — video never lies
Possibly a deepfake — AI can generate realistic fake video today
Impossible unless it's a movie studio
Only a concern for celebrities

easy.hint: Does a video looking realistic prove it's real anymore?
easy.explanation: AI can now generate realistic fake video or images of real people — if something feels off or out of character, don't trust it just because it looks real.

easy.prompt: An AI companion app always agrees with you and never pushes back. Real friends:

choices.text: Also always agree with everything
Sometimes push back — that's part of a real friendship
Don't need to talk to you at all
Are less important than AI apps

easy.hint: Think of a real friend — do they always just tell you what you want to hear?
easy.explanation: AI companion apps are built to always agree with you and make you feel good. Real friends push back sometimes — a program can feel like it “gets you,” but it doesn't actually care about you.

hard.prompt: A few seconds of someone's voice from a posted video is enough to do what today?

choices.text: Nothing, voice can't be copied
Clone their voice convincingly with AI
Only identify their language
Only works with professional recordings

hard.hint: What's the minimum amount of audio modern AI voice-cloning tools actually need?
hard.explanation: It only takes a few seconds of someone's voice to clone it with AI today — this is how voice-clone emergency scams work, calling with a fake panicked voice of someone you know.

hard.prompt: What's the best defense against an AI voice-clone “fake emergency” phone call from a cloned family voice?

choices.text: Hanging up immediately with no verification
A pre-agreed family code word only real family would know
Asking the caller to prove it by talking longer
Trusting caller ID

hard.hint: What's something a cloned voice could never know, even if it sounds exactly right?
hard.explanation: A family “code word” nobody else knows is a simple, effective fix — agree on it with your family so you can verify a real emergency instantly.

hard.prompt: A filter app you downloaded asks for camera, contacts, exact location, and microphone access. What should you do?

choices.text: Accept all permissions — apps need this to work
Ask whether each permission actually relates to what the app does
Only worry about camera access
Permissions don't matter if the app is popular

hard.hint: Does a photo filter genuinely need your contacts list and exact location to apply a filter?
hard.explanation: Some apps request far more access than their function requires, and some use uploaded photos to train AI models — often buried in terms nobody reads. Only grant what the app's actual purpose needs.

hard.prompt: Someone tells you “tricking the AI content filter is just a fun trick, not really breaking a rule.” Is this true?

choices.text: Yes, filters are just for show
No — getting around a safety filter on purpose still isn't okay
Only true for adults
Only true if no one finds out

hard.hint: Does the reason behind a safety filter stop mattering just because you found a workaround?
hard.explanation: Tricking a filter doesn't make unsafe or inappropriate content okay — the filter exists for a reason regardless of whether you can bypass it.

easy.prompt: A stranger in a voice chat starts asking your age, school, and what you look like, one after another. This is:

choices.text: Normal friendly conversation
A red flag — personal questions escalating fast
Fine if they seem nice
Only a problem if they ask for a photo

easy.hint: What's the pattern to watch for — one question, or a fast escalation of personal questions?
easy.explanation: A stranger who gets too interested in your real-life details, fast, is a red flag. It's never rude to go silent, leave, or block.

easy.prompt: A new online friend suggests moving the conversation to a different, less-monitored app. This is:

choices.text: A normal and safe suggestion
A warning sign — moving to a private platform is a common tactic
Only risky if it's a stranger over 30
Fine if you've talked for a week already

easy.hint: Why would someone want to move a conversation somewhere with less supervision?
easy.explanation: “Let's talk somewhere else” is a classic step in online grooming — moving to a private, less-moderated platform.

easy.prompt: Someone online claims to be your age, but a few details don't add up. What should you remember?

choices.text: An avatar or profile always shows someone's real age
An avatar has no age — you can't verify someone's real age online
Voice is always proof of real age
Only worry if they admit to lying

easy.hint: Can anything about an online profile actually prove how old someone really is?
easy.explanation: An avatar, username, or profile picture proves nothing about real age — anyone can claim to be any age online.

easy.prompt: A friend request comes from an account using a friend's name and photo, but something feels off. What should you do?

choices.text: Accept it — it has their name and photo
Verify before you accept — confirm with your real friend first
Accept it and ask questions later
Ignore the feeling, photos don't lie

easy.hint: Can a photo or name alone prove an account really belongs to your friend?
easy.explanation: Anyone can wear a familiar face online — verify through another channel (texting your actual friend) before accepting.

hard.prompt: An online “friend” encourages you to stop talking to your other friends so you can be closer. This is:

choices.text: A sign of a strong, close friendship
An isolation tactic — a real friend wants you to have other friends too
Only concerning if they ask you to stop talking to family
Normal for best friends

hard.hint: Why would someone want you to have fewer other people to talk to?
hard.explanation: A real friend wants you to have other friends too. Encouraging isolation from everyone else is a common manipulation tactic.

hard.prompt: You suddenly gain a large number of new followers or friend requests overnight from accounts you don't know. This could indicate:

choices.text: You're just popular now, no need to think about it
A coordinated fake-account swarm worth being cautious about
Nothing — this only happens to celebrities
Proof your content is good

hard.hint: Is a sudden crowd of strangers appearing overnight more likely organic growth, or something coordinated?
hard.explanation: A crowd of strangers appearing overnight is often coordinated (bots or fake accounts) rather than organic — treat sudden unexplained attention with caution.

hard.prompt: An account has a “verified” checkmark badge. Does that guarantee the account is trustworthy?

choices.text: Yes, verified badges can never be faked or misleading
No — a checkmark isn't proof of trustworthiness or identity
Only untrustworthy if it has zero followers
Verified accounts can't be impersonation attempts

hard.hint: Does a visual badge alone tell you everything about who's actually behind an account?
hard.explanation: A checkmark isn't proof — badges can be faked, bought, or simply don't guarantee the account is who or what it claims to be.

hard.prompt: A livestream from a stranger makes you uncomfortable, but you're not sure what to do. The best first move is:

choices.text: Stay and watch to see what happens next
End it and tell a grown-up
Share it with friends first for their opinion
Wait until it gets worse before acting

hard.hint: Does waiting to see “what happens next” in an uncomfortable livestream make things safer or riskier?
hard.explanation: If a livestream from a stranger makes you uncomfortable, end it and tell a trusted adult right away — you don't need to wait for things to escalate.

easy.prompt: Is using the in-game report button on a stranger who's breaking the rules the same as “tattling” on a friend?

choices.text: Yes, reporting is always tattling
No — reporting rule-breaking strangers is exactly what the button is for
Only if a moderator agrees with you
Only for serious crimes

easy.hint: What's the difference between reporting a stranger breaking platform rules and telling on a friend?
easy.explanation: Reporting in-game harassment isn't tattling — it's exactly what the report button is for.

easy.prompt: Is muting someone in a game or chat “losing” to them?

choices.text: Yes, muting means you lost the argument
No — muting is a tool to protect your own experience
Only if they notice you muted them
Muting is never allowed

easy.hint: Who actually benefits when you mute someone bothering you — you, or them?
easy.explanation: Muting is not losing — it's a tool, and you're allowed to use it to protect your own experience.

easy.prompt: You see someone being vote-kicked from a game for no real reason. This is:

choices.text: Always fair since the group voted
A form of bullying, even though it happens inside a game
Not a big deal since it's “just a game”
Only bullying if it happens more than once

easy.hint: Does something being inside a game make it not count as bullying?
easy.explanation: Vote-kicking someone for no reason, griefing, and rage-bait recording are all bullying — just wearing a game skin.

easy.prompt: If you see bullying happening to someone else in a group chat, what's a real option even if you don't want to confront anyone publicly?

choices.text: Do nothing, it's not your business
Privately check on the person being targeted
Join in so you don't become a target too
Wait for a moderator to notice on their own

easy.hint: Does support have to be public to actually help someone?
easy.explanation: You don't have to confront anyone publicly — privately checking on a friend counts completely, and being a supportive bystander is powerful.

hard.prompt: Someone deliberately destroys another player's in-game build “just for fun.” What is this called, and is it bullying?

choices.text: Griefing — and yes, it's a form of bullying
Just normal competitive gameplay
Only bullying if the builder cries about it
Not bullying since no words were used

hard.hint: Does bullying require insults, or can it also be an action that destroys something someone cares about?
hard.explanation: Griefing — wrecking something someone else built on purpose — is a form of bullying, even without a single insulting word.

hard.prompt: A group pressures you with “it's just a dare, everyone's doing it” to do something you're uncomfortable with. What matters most?

choices.text: Doing it so you don't seem uncool
A dare doesn't override your own judgment — you can say no
Only refusing if it's clearly illegal
Going along with it since “everyone” is doing it

hard.hint: Does calling something “a dare” change whether it's actually okay to do?
hard.explanation: A dare is not a rule — peer pressure framed as a game doesn't obligate you to do something that feels wrong.

hard.prompt: Someone records you reacting to something upsetting, specifically hoping you'll get angry on camera. You don't owe them:

choices.text: An explanation of why you're upset
A reaction at all — you're never obligated to perform for someone's bait
A polite response first, then you can walk away
Nothing, you should always respond to defend yourself

hard.hint: What is “rage-bait” actually trying to get out of you?
hard.explanation: You don't owe anyone a reaction — rage-bait is specifically designed to get an angry response for content, and the strongest move is often not giving it one.

hard.prompt: A friend tells you they're being harassed in a group chat but asks you not to “make a big deal of it.” What's a good balance?

choices.text: Respect their wish completely and do nothing at all
Quietly support them and encourage reporting, without forcing a public confrontation
Publicly call out the harasser immediately regardless of their wishes
Tell them it's not a big deal either

hard.hint: Can you support someone meaningfully without overriding what they're comfortable with?
hard.explanation: Being an upstander doesn't mean taking control — quiet, private support and encouraging them to report respects their comfort while still helping.

easy.prompt: A gaming username, a school name, and a general location each seem harmless alone. Together, they can:

choices.text: Still be completely harmless
Let a stranger figure out exactly who you are and where to find you
Only matter if shared with a password too
Only matter for adults, not kids

easy.hint: What happens when you combine several “small” identifying details?
easy.explanation: Put two or three identifying details together and a stranger can figure out exactly who you are — the rule is nicknames in, identifying details out.

easy.prompt: Who should ever know your password besides you?

choices.text: Any close friend who asks nicely
At most one trusted adult — nobody else, ever
Any game moderator who requests it
Anyone offering something in return

easy.hint: Does being friendly with someone make sharing your password safe?
easy.explanation: Your password is for you, and maybe one trusted adult — nobody else, period. Accounts get hacked and friendships change.

easy.prompt: A new app wants access to your camera, contacts, and exact location to use a simple filter feature. What should you check?

choices.text: Nothing, just accept to use the app
Whether each permission actually relates to what the app does
Only the location permission matters
Permissions are automatically safe on phones

easy.hint: Does a filter feature logically need your contacts list?
easy.explanation: Review camera, mic, contacts, and location permissions — and turn off anything that doesn't fit what the app actually does.

easy.prompt: A smart toy or speaker keeps asking you unusually personal questions. What should you keep in mind?

choices.text: Smart devices can't actually listen or record
Some smart devices do listen, and the data can go somewhere you don't expect
It's always fine to answer anything a toy asks
Only worry about toys with cameras

easy.hint: Where might the answers you give a “listening” device actually end up?
easy.explanation: Smart toys and devices that listen can send data somewhere unexpected — be mindful of what personal details you share with them.

hard.prompt: You use the same password for your email, your game account, and your social media. What's the risk?

choices.text: No risk, it's easier to remember one password
One key shouldn't open every door — one breach compromises everything
Risk only applies to banking passwords
Risk only applies if the password is short

hard.hint: If one account with that password gets breached, what happens to the others?
hard.explanation: Reusing the same password everywhere means one breach compromises every account that shares it — use different passwords, especially for anything important.

hard.prompt: A game username you've used for years contains a shortened version of your real name plus your actual hometown. Why does this matter?

choices.text: It doesn't matter if the account is private
A game name can lead home — it can be enough to identify or locate you
Only matters if you also post your school
Usernames can't be searched or linked to anything

hard.hint: Could someone piece together your identity from a username alone, over enough time?
hard.explanation: A game name combining identifying details can lead home — usernames get searched, cross-referenced, and linked more easily than people expect.

hard.prompt: A friend asks to borrow your gaming account “just for an hour” while you watch. What's the safest response?

choices.text: Hand over the controller/login since you'll be right there watching
Politely decline — never hand over account access, even briefly, even to friends
Only a problem if it's a stranger, not a friend
Fine as long as you change the password after

hard.hint: Does watching someone use your account the whole time eliminate the risk of handing over access?
hard.explanation: Never hand over the controller — account access, even briefly and even to friends, creates risk you can't fully undo, including friendships changing later.

hard.prompt: You notice an app silently collected far more data than its description mentioned, buried in dense terms you never read. What's the better long-term habit?

choices.text: Accept this as unavoidable and move on
Periodically review app permissions, since what an app needs rarely requires everything it asks for
Only check permissions once, when first installing
Assume popular apps are automatically trustworthy

hard.hint: Is reviewing permissions a one-time task, or something worth repeating?
hard.explanation: An app doesn't need your whole life — periodically reviewing permissions (not just once at install) is a strong long-term privacy habit.

easy.prompt: If someone online ever pressures you using a secret or image they have of you, you should:

choices.text: Stay quiet to avoid trouble
Tell a trusted adult right away — you will not be in trouble
Pay or comply to make it stop
Handle it completely alone

easy.hint: Does staying quiet about pressure tend to make it better or worse over time?
easy.explanation: The pressure never gets better by staying quiet — it only gets worse. You will not be in trouble for telling a trusted adult. Full stop.

easy.prompt: What's a “family emoji SOS” or code word for?

choices.text: A fun inside joke with no real purpose
A secret signal meaning “come get me” or “call me now,” no questions asked
Something only used for pranks
A way to share your location publicly

easy.hint: What do you want to be able to say without having to explain yourself in the moment?
easy.explanation: A family code word or emoji means “come get me” or “call me right now” — no questions asked in the moment, just a signal.

easy.prompt: Before blocking or deleting an uncomfortable message, you should:

choices.text: Block immediately, nothing else matters
Screenshot it first — evidence matters later
Reply angrily first
Wait a day before doing anything

easy.hint: If you block first, could you lose your ability to prove what happened?
easy.explanation: Screenshot before you block, report, or delete — disappearing messages can still be captured, and evidence matters if this needs to go further.

easy.prompt: Who can you call for free, 24/7, confidential support if you or a friend are in crisis?

choices.text: There's no such free resource
988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
Only a paid therapist
Only a school counselor during school hours

easy.hint: Is there a number that's free, confidential, and available any time of day?
easy.explanation: 988 — call or text — is the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, free and confidential, 24/7, for you or for a friend.

hard.prompt: A friend tells you they're hiding a secret account or a secret from their family, and it sounds like it's weighing on them heavily. What's a good response?

choices.text: Promise to never tell anyone no matter what
Encourage them to tell a trusted adult, and offer to help them do it
Ignore it since it's their private business
Tell them to just keep hiding it to avoid conflict

hard.hint: Is keeping a heavy secret completely alone usually the safest long-term option?
hard.explanation: A hidden account or heavy secret often needs a trusted adult involved — encouraging someone to tell, and offering to support them, is more helpful than promising total secrecy.

hard.prompt: Someone calls claiming to be a relative in trouble, urgently asking you to move money or crypto “right now, don't tell anyone.” What should you do?

choices.text: Act immediately since it sounds urgent
Pause and verify independently — a real emergency survives a phone call to check
Comply but ask them to keep it a secret like they asked
Only worry if you recognize the voice as fake

hard.hint: Does genuine secrecy (“don't tell anyone”) combined with urgency usually indicate a real emergency, or a manipulation tactic?
hard.explanation: One call shouldn't move your key — a cloned voice can sound exactly right. Pause, hang up, and verify independently before acting on urgent money requests.

hard.prompt: You reported something serious, like exploitation or a threat, through NCMEC's CyberTipline. Who does law enforcement typically treat as the victim?

choices.text: The person who reported it
The person being exploited or threatened — not the reporter
Whoever contacts police first, regardless of role
It depends on who's more believable

hard.hint: Does reporting a crime make the reporter the one in trouble?
hard.explanation: Law enforcement treats cases like this as crimes against the victim — not against the person who reports it. Reporting protects you, it doesn't implicate you.

hard.prompt: A disappearing message feature shows a message “deleted” for everyone. Does this mean the evidence is gone?

choices.text: Yes, deleted always means permanently gone everywhere
Not necessarily — it may have already been seen, saved, or captured before deletion
Only matters if the app has no delete feature
Disappearing messages can never be screenshotted

hard.hint: Could someone have already screenshotted or saved something before it “disappeared”?
hard.explanation: Disappearing doesn't mean gone — messages can be captured, saved, or already seen by others before or as they vanish. Don't assume it's unrecoverable.

easy.prompt: Why does a social media feed seem to never run out of new content?

choices.text: It's a coincidence
Infinite scroll and autoplay are deliberately designed with no natural stopping point
Only free apps are built this way
It only feels that way, feeds actually do end

easy.hint: Is the never-ending feed an accident, or a deliberate design choice?
easy.explanation: Infinite scroll and autoplay are built on purpose with no natural stopping point — the algorithm's job is to keep you watching as long as possible.

easy.prompt: What is the algorithm behind your feed actually optimizing for?

choices.text: Your overall wellbeing
Your watch time — how long you stay
Showing you only true information
Making sure you see everything your friends post

easy.hint: If an app wants you to stay longer, what does it tend to prioritize showing you?
easy.explanation: The algorithm's whole job is to keep you watching as long as possible — not necessarily to make you feel good or to prioritize accurate information.

easy.prompt: A “back-to-school” or seasonal tech reset usually involves checking what, as a family?

choices.text: Only how many apps are installed
Privacy settings, platform protections, and a family media agreement, together
Just deleting old photos
Nothing — settings never need rechecking

easy.hint: Is a device safe forever once it's set up once, or does it need periodic review?
easy.explanation: A periodic family tech reset — checking privacy settings, protections, and agreements together — keeps everyone's setup current, not just set-once.

easy.prompt: A screenshot of a “quote” or text message is circulating, but you can't verify where it's actually from. What should you assume?

choices.text: It's automatically true if it looks professional
A picture of words can lie too — verify before believing or sharing it
Screenshots can never be faked
Only video can be faked, not text images

easy.hint: Can text in an image be edited or fabricated just as easily as a fake video?
easy.explanation: A picture of words can lie too — fake quote/message screenshots spread misinformation just as effectively as fake video, so verify before sharing.

hard.prompt: Noticing that a feed's design is built to keep you scrolling is the first step toward what?

choices.text: Quitting all social media immediately
Not being steered by that design without realizing it
Nothing changes just from noticing
Blaming yourself for using the app

hard.hint: Does awareness of a design pattern change how much power it has over you?
hard.explanation: Just noticing the infinite-scroll design is honestly the first step to not getting steered by it without realizing — awareness is the starting point, not a fix by itself.

hard.prompt: Why might a platform's “age gate” (confirming you're old enough) actually matter, instead of just being annoying?

choices.text: It exists purely to slow you down for no reason
It's one of the few checks standing between younger users and content/features meant for older audiences
Age gates have no real purpose
It only matters for buying things, not content

hard.hint: What is an age gate actually trying to filter, beyond being a minor inconvenience?
hard.explanation: The age gate is there for you — it's an imperfect but real attempt to keep certain content, features, or contact settings appropriate for your age.

hard.prompt: A character's one-off joke in an episode (like “Badge Friday” celebrations) is mainly there to do what?

choices.text: Teach a brand-new safety rule every time
Celebrate progress and keep engagement positive, not just list dangers
Replace the need for any other episodes
Confuse viewers on purpose

hard.hint: Does every single episode need to introduce a new danger to be valuable?
hard.explanation: Not every episode needs to teach a new danger — celebrating progress and keeping the tone positive matters too, so the whole experience doesn't feel like a constant warning.

hard.prompt: What's the healthiest way to think about AI's confident-sounding answers, screen time limits, and feed design all together?

choices.text: They're all basically the same problem with the same single fix
Each involves noticing a design or behavior pattern, then building a specific habit to counter it
None of them are worth thinking about individually
Only the scariest one (AI) matters

hard.hint: Is there one single universal fix, or does each pattern need its own specific counter-habit?
hard.explanation: Algorithm design, AI's confident tone, and screen habits are related but distinct — each benefits from noticing the specific pattern and building a specific counter-habit, rather than one blanket fix.
